context:
dev-flow is a Claude Code plugin implementing a five-station software development methodology: Intake, Decide, Spec, Build, Ship. Decide, Spec, and Ship each end in a gate (G1, G2, G3); Intake and Build have completion criteria but no gate letter. Gate verdicts (PASS/REQUEST_CHANGES/HOLD) are signed through an ordered fallback chain: a qualified human reviewer first, a fresh-context reviewer agent second, the project owner's own self-review as a last resort, with the rule that the author of a change may not also be its approver. Only the Ship station is a default human stop point today; the other stations already route substantial verification work through models and scripts.

The plugin's sole maintainer ("the owner") has described a preferred flow, in his own words: work should start immediately once an intake interview ends; only the Ship-station demo should be shown to a human, and only when a human asks for it; genuinely unclear requirements should be resolved before execution rather than after; execution should be followed automatically by an end-to-end verification pass; the verification evidence produced at the end of a feature should be judged by an automated router; a human's feedback on that judgment should come last, after the fact; and over time the amount of human-in-the-loop review should shrink.

jev is a hosted, closed-weight classification API from TypeSafe AI ("System One"), released into early access roughly one week before this evaluation. It takes a text or JSON "state" plus one or more typed questions (yes/no, multiple-choice, or ordered-scale) and returns calibrated probability distributions, not free text. TypeSafe's own documentation states: "Calibration is measured across groups of predictions; it does not guarantee that an individual answer is correct." Every packet sent to jev leaves the local machine as an HTTPS request to a third-party API; there is no self-hosted or open-weight version, and no independent benchmark of its accuracy was found.

The repository already has several purely mechanical guards relevant to any jev integration: a "reviewer-selection" clause describing the human-first-then-agent-then-owner approval chain is kept byte-for-byte in sync across five separate files by an automated consistency checker; the Ship-station demo verdict is rejected by a script unless it carries a literal human-attestation line, with no agent-authored exception; and the project's stated verification laws include one specifying that Owner Calls — decisions the project owner alone may make — may never be answered on the owner's behalf by an agent, human reviewer, or automated router.

forks.title: Which integration point goes live first
forks.decision: In what order should the J1 intake-clarity check, the J3 demo recommendation, and J5 Ship-gate shadow-mode recording be built and shipped relative to one another?
facts: J1 sits at the Intake-to-Decide boundary; its evidence packet is limited to three existing sections of `1-discussion.md` (the Real-world Context section, the three-state Open Questions list, and the Interview Log's conclusion column), not the full conversation transcript. The Interview Log itself is capped at eight entries and each conclusion is tagged CONFIRMED, NEEDS_VERIFICATION, or OPEN, so the packet J1 reads is already a short, structured summary rather than raw dialogue (R3-process §2).

J5 sits at the Ship gate and evaluates the largest evidence packet among the six integration points examined in this evaluation: Final Fresh Run's per-layer table, Evidence Gauntlet E1-E13, the two-axis review (Standards and Spec axes), and, if a separate mandatory-check fork is adopted, an e2e summary. Assembling this packet correctly is described in the original proposal as the single largest piece of engineering effort in the whole design (R3-process §1, §4; draft §5).

During shadow mode, the gate's actual sign-off (`route_taken`) is always the pre-existing fallback behavior; jev's recommendation is recorded but never changes what a human or fallback agent signs. This holds for every gate discussed in this evaluation, not only the ones examined in this fork, and is the reason shadow-period data is treated elsewhere in this evaluation as the only unbiased source of comparison labels (R4-calib §0.2).

R2-risk's adversarial review argues that none of the seven safety guards examined elsewhere in this evaluation should be skipped for shadow-mode calls specifically, since shadow mode still transmits evidence packets to a third-party API and writes ledger rows that later become graduation samples; a guard gap during shadow mode is, in this framing, still a live data-handling risk even though no routing decision is at stake (R2-risk B1, B5, closing section).

R2-risk's closing section states that six of the seven guards (a seventh, verdict-authorship auditability, is a distinct, later-identified item) are a precondition it considers necessary before any script code is written at all: "if these six groups are not done, P1 should not even start writing devflow-jev.py" (R2-risk, closing section, translated). The review frames this as the single most load-bearing recommendation in its entire report.

R3-process's process review recommends building J1 and J3 in the same window as, rather than strictly after, the shared script/ledger infrastructure, reasoning that J4/J5-in-shadow produces no perceptible difference for the owner while it runs, whereas J1 and J3 are described as the two levers that map directly onto something the owner said he wanted, out of six integration points examined across the evaluation (R3-process §4; §1).

The original 0-draft's phase table proposed P0 (draft plus smoke test) → P1 (shared script, ledger, observability, with J4 and J5 running in shadow mode plus e2e templates) → P2 (J1 clarity routing and J3 demo recommendation, live) → P3 (contract changes for J2/J5 automatic routing), with P2's live features gated only on the owner subjectively judging the P2-phase output reasonable, not on any statistical threshold (draft §8, phase table).

Historical feature throughput recorded in the project's own status tracking is, per R3-process's review, on the order of single digits per month, and the project's own Active-feature tracking table was empty at the time of review; R3-process uses this, as an estimate rather than a measured figure, to project that a single gate's sample threshold discussed in a separate fork could take on the order of a quarter to a year to reach (R3-process §4).

At least one reviewer (R3-process) recommends completing a separate, jev-independent mandatory e2e verification check before J5 shadow-mode sampling begins, to avoid mixing two different evidence-packet shapes inside one sample pool; whether that recommendation is followed is a separate, undecided question examined elsewhere in this evaluation (R3-process §5).

Shared infrastructure — the `devflow-jev.py` script (four subcommands: pack, ask, feedback, report), the question-set registry, and the ledger file format — is a prerequisite for every J-point regardless of which one ships first, meaning none of this fork's three options avoids building it (draft §6).

Neither J1 nor J3 requires any shadow-mode sample accumulation before going live; the 0-draft classifies both as additive changes that could go live directly, without an accumulation period, once the shared script and guards exist, in contrast to J5's automatic-ship path, which is explicitly gated on a statistical threshold examined in a separate fork (draft §7 table).

J1's specific mechanism — translating a jev-flagged "weakest dimension" into a new `/dev-talk` session — requires a full eleven-step dev-talk cycle, including a mandatory human nod at node N13 and regenerating the session's rendered HTML output, each time it triggers, not a single follow-up question, because dev-talk's own rule states a new session "never continues from the previous one" (R3-process §2, quoting `skills/dev-talk/SKILL.md` node N13-end).

R3-process's review recommends capping J1's re-ask loop at two rounds before falling back to an existing three-way outcome that routes the remaining ambiguity to a single human question, specifically to bound how many full eleven-step dev-talk cycles one clarity check can trigger before defaulting to asking the owner directly (R3-process §2).

The J4 build-stage routing point (failure classification and model-tier escalation) is unaffected by this fork's ordering choice; all four reviews and the draft describe it as independently scoped, low-risk, purely additive work with no dependency on J1, J3, or J5, since no human is in that loop today regardless of jev's involvement (draft §4 J4 row; devflow-state (a) rows 8-9).

None of the three options in this fork change what a human or fallback agent ever signs at any gate; the only thing this fork decides is the order in which three pieces of engineering work — a small packet, a small packet, and the largest packet in the evaluation — are scheduled relative to each other. Whichever option is chosen, all three deliverables (J1, J3, J5-shadow) still require the same seven safety guards examined in a separate fork to protect the data those deliverables send or record; this fork's ordering choice does not change how many guards must exist, only when each deliverable's own packet-handling code is written relative to the others (draft §7 table; R2-risk closing section).

A.description: Build the J1 clarity check and the J5 shadow-mode recording in the same development window, so both become available at roughly the same time rather than one finishing well before the other. Shared infrastructure such as the script, ledger, and question-set registry is built once and exercised by both from the start.
for: A single engineering pass can build the shared script, ledger, and question-set registry once against both J1's small packet and J5's large packet, rather than validating the shared pipeline twice against packets of very different sizes and possibly discovering packet-size-related bugs a second time. That saves a second round of debugging a packet-size-related bug that had already been fixed once, in the packet size first encountered.

Because J5 shadow accumulation is calendar-bound rather than effort-bound, starting its clock at the same time as J1 rather than strictly after it begins accumulating toward later thresholds sooner, which matters because sample accumulation cannot be sped up by adding more engineering effort (R3-process §4).

Because all seven safety guards examined elsewhere in this evaluation must be complete before either J1 or J5-shadow can begin, and that guard work is shared infrastructure independent of which J-point starts first, building the two together does not, by itself, add extra guard-related work beyond what either ordering would already require.

Neither J1 nor J5-shadow depends on the other's evidence packet or question set, so building them in parallel does not create a sequencing dependency between the two pieces of work themselves, only a scheduling choice about developer attention (draft §4, J1 and J5 rows, independent packet definitions).
against: R3-process's review found no technical dependency forcing J1 and J5-shadow to build together, and recommended prioritizing J1/J3 precisely because they, unlike J5, produce a difference the owner can feel while the shared infrastructure is still being built (R3-process §4). The review frames this as the clearest available signal for sequencing, since it is drawn directly from the owner's own words rather than from an inference about packet difficulty.

Building both at once means the first deliverable does not exist until both the small J1 packet and the far larger J5 packet are ready together; R3-process's review frames validating the shared pipeline against the cheaper packet first as lower-risk than validating it against the two at once (R3-process §4). That risk falls specifically on the shared pipeline's first real exercise, since neither packet has been validated against it before this option begins.

If R2-risk's position that all guards relevant to shadow-mode calls must be complete before any shadow-mode code runs is adopted, building J1 and J5-shadow together does not shorten that shared guard-completion critical path, since the guards themselves remain the limiting step regardless of how the two deliverables are scheduled around them (R2-risk closing section).

Splitting developer attention across the small J1 packet and the large J5 packet at the same time risks the larger, more error-prone packet-assembly work (the draft's own description of J5's evidence packet as the largest engineering effort) absorbing review and debugging time that would otherwise go toward shipping J1 sooner (draft §5; R3-process §1).

B.description: Ship the J1 intake-clarity check live first, then the J3 demo-worth-it recommendation, and only after both are live and validated begin recording J5 shadow-mode samples at the Ship gate. Each piece becomes usable to the owner in sequence, one after another, rather than arriving at the same time.
for: R3-process's review recommends exactly this ordering, describing J1 and J3 as the only two levers that produce an immediately felt difference on what the owner explicitly said he wanted, unlike J4/J5-in-shadow, which it describes as imperceptible to the owner while it runs (R3-process §4). No other option in this fork is described as directly by any of the four reviews as matching the owner's own stated preferences.

J1's evidence packet is limited to three small existing sections of `1-discussion.md`, versus J5's substantially larger packet; validating the shared script/ledger/question-set pipeline against the cheaper packet before tackling the larger one is, per R3-process's review, the lower-risk order (R3-process §4; §1). Assembling J5's packet correctly is, by the draft's own account, the largest single piece of engineering effort anywhere in this evaluation.

Shipping J1 and J3 first means the owner experiences a difference in his workflow while J5's evidence-packet assembly — described in the original proposal as the largest piece of engineering effort in the whole design — is still in progress, rather than only after that larger effort completes (R3-process §1, §4; draft §5).

Sequencing the two small, self-contained deliverables ahead of the one large, more failure-prone one means any bug discovered while building J1 or J3 is isolated to a small packet and a short feedback loop, rather than surfacing for the first time inside the largest and most complex packet in the evaluation.
against: J5 shadow-mode sample accumulation runs on calendar time rather than engineering effort; delaying its start until after two other deliverables ship means its threshold, discussed in a separate fork, is reached correspondingly later, and that delay cannot be recovered later by working faster (R3-process §4).

Separately from this fork's ordering question, at least one reviewer recommends that an e2e mandatory-check finish before J5 shadow sampling begins at all; if that recommendation is followed, it would add to J5's own lead time regardless of which J-point this fork places first (R3-process §5).

If all seven safety guards examined elsewhere in this evaluation are required to be complete, with negative tests, before any of J1, J3, or J5-shadow can ship, this fork's ordering choice does not change that shared blocking requirement, since it would apply under any sequence (R2-risk closing section).

A strictly sequential build means the shared script, ledger, and question-set registry are validated first only against J1 and J3's comparatively simple packets, deferring discovery of any issue specific to J5's much larger packet shape until after two other deliverables have already shipped. That deferred discovery risk applies specifically to J5's packet, since J1 and J3's smaller packets are validated first under this option.

C.description: Begin J5 shadow-mode recording first, before J1 or J3 go live, because its sample accumulation runs on calendar time and any delay in starting it delays reaching the sample thresholds examined in a separate fork. J1 and J3 follow once J5 shadow recording is underway.
for: J5's sample accumulation is calendar-bound rather than engineering-bound; R3-process's review estimates, as a projection rather than a measured figure, that reaching the threshold discussed in a separate fork could take on the order of a quarter to a year once shadow recording begins, so starting that clock earlier reaches the threshold correspondingly earlier (R3-process §4).

Starting the calendar-bound item first and the engineering-bound items (J1, J3) afterward means the two do not compete for the same development window, and the longest-lead-time item is not left waiting behind two shorter items that could otherwise ship while its clock is already running.

None of J5's shadow-mode behavior changes what a human signs at the Ship gate — the recommendation is recorded but the actual sign-off stays exactly as it is today during shadow mode (R4-calib §0.2) — so starting it first carries no routing-behavior risk relative to the status quo. No routing-behavior risk arises under this option specifically because shadow mode's sign-off behavior is identical no matter which J-point starts first.

Because J5's evidence packet is the largest and most complex in the evaluation, building and debugging it first, while developer attention is freshest and before two other deliverables have consumed part of the same window, may surface packet-assembly problems earlier than a later, more divided schedule would (draft §5).
against: R3-process's review found J5-shadow produces no felt difference for the owner while it runs, describing it as entirely background record-keeping that does not change any behavior; sequencing it first means the two changes the owner explicitly described wanting (intake and demo) are delayed behind a change he cannot perceive (R3-process §4).

J5's evidence packet is, per R3-process's review, larger and more complex to assemble correctly than J1's three small sections; validating the shared script/ledger/question-set pipeline against the hardest packet first is a higher-risk order than validating it against the simplest packet first (R3-process §4). Validating the pipeline against the hardest packet first also means any bug found there delays every deliverable built afterward, not only J5.

At least one reviewer (R3-process) recommends completing an e2e mandatory-check before J5 shadow sampling begins, to avoid mixing evidence-packet shapes within the sample pool discussed in a separate fork; if that recommendation is followed, J5 shadow could not literally be first in the way this option describes (R3-process §5).

Delaying J1 and J3 behind J5-shadow means the two integration points R3-process's review maps directly onto the owner's own stated preferences are the last, not the first, of the three to reach the owner, even though building them does not require any of J5's larger packet-assembly work to exist first (R3-process §1, §4).

forks.title: Where the jev ledger lives
forks.decision: Which existing (or new) storage mechanism should hold the jev ledger that records every call and its later human label?
facts: The repository's durable memory subsystem writes to `.dev-flow/` through exactly one entry point and one trigger moment: `memory/agentmem/durable.py`'s write functions (covering decisions, knowledge, implementation state, and events), called only from `sync.consolidate()` at checkpoint or session-end. A local, disposable SQLite cache also exists alongside this durable tree, but it is explicitly rebuildable from `.dev-flow/` and is not itself part of the durable, git-tracked record (devflow-state (b), "durable writes have only one entry point and one moment").

The existing episodic-event store, `.dev-flow/events/YYYY/MM/<session_id>.jsonl`, is split one file per session specifically to avoid concurrent-append corruption across machines, and this store is one of five distinct file families that together make up the git-tracked `.dev-flow/` durable memory, alongside decisions, knowledge, implementation state, and skills (devflow-state (b) table).

R2-risk's adversarial review independently identified the same concurrency failure mode for a single shared ledger file: parallel review candidates each calling `ask` and appending to one `ledger.jsonl` reproduces the append-collision problem the events store was split to avoid, risking silent loss of feedback or ask records during concurrent Wave Review sessions (R2-risk B4).

The observability run stream (`.devflow/runs/<run_id>/...`) cannot be used for J1, J2, or J3: `hooks/_obs_impl.py` fail-closes whenever no `run_id` exists, and `run_id` is created only by the Build-stage execution guard, which Intake/Decide/Spec-stage code never calls; the underlying design explicitly states the system does not guess or self-create a run, and the exact wording R1-arch quotes from the implementation is a hard failure message telling the caller to arm the guard first rather than attempting to proceed (R1-arch, coupling table, J1/J2/J3 row).

Whether J5 (the Ship-gate integration point) has an observability run available at the moment its final verdict is signed is explicitly unconfirmed: R1-arch's initial judgment that J5 was clean was withdrawn on a second reading of the Build/Ship handoff, which shows the Build-stage run being stopped before the Ship station begins, alongside an ambiguous separate reference to the Ship station opening its own run whose closing point was not directly read (R1-arch, "J5 run_id timing" section, marked unconfirmed).

R1-arch found that writing jev's outcome into observability events exactly as the draft originally described (an `agent_role: verifier` field alongside a `model` field) is not purely additive: the schema's forbidden-field list excludes `model`/`agent_role` from the two event types a verifier-role writer may emit, so this would require either a schema change or folding the outcome into a free-text summary field of roughly 2,000 characters, losing field-level queryability for any reporting tool (R1-arch Q2).

A grep pass over the two scripts that assert architecture invariants for `.dev-flow/` found no rule blocking a second writer from creating new files under `.dev-flow/`; both scripts' relevant checks concern the existing writer's own internal correctness (gitignore exclusion, write ordering, symlink safety), not a general "only one writer allowed" guard — but this was a grep pass on two files of roughly 2,750 and 1,150 lines respectively, not a full read, so confidence is medium. Both reviews that looked at this question independently flagged the same two files as needing a full read before implementation begins, rather than treating the grep result as a settled answer (R3-process §8; R1-arch, unscanned-files list).

R3-process's review recommends extending the existing append-only event function with a new event kind rather than opening a new `.dev-flow/jev/` namespace, reasoning that the memory subsystem should keep exactly one write-timing model (checkpoint/session-end) rather than gain a second, "whenever called" timing model that behaves differently from every other durable artifact in the same directory (R3-process §8).

Whether the existing append-only event function can accept a custom event kind at all — the technical precondition for that recommendation — is explicitly listed as an unresolved item still to be settled by direct testing, corroborated by R1-arch's and R3-process's shared note that the relevant implementation file was not fully read by either review.

A ledger entry written at the instant a jev call completes falls entirely outside the existing consolidate-time write path; nothing today would commit a bare new file under `.dev-flow/jev/` into git unless a new step is added somewhere in the feature-completion sequence, since the consolidation function's call graph is the only mechanism that currently commits new durable files. This gap exists independent of which of this fork's three options is chosen, since even reusing the existing event function still routes through the same consolidation timing rather than committing at call time (R1-arch Q3).

The project's own end-of-Build durability check treats any uncommitted new file under the durable root the same way regardless of which subsystem wrote it, using a full-tree `git status --porcelain -uall` scan; an uncommitted jev ledger file would legitimately fail that check unless a commit step for it is added somewhere in the wrap-up sequence, and this is a correct application of an existing rule rather than a misdetection (R1-arch Q3).

R1-arch reports finding zero existing lines of code in the scripts, hooks, memory, or observability directories that open an outbound network connection to a non-localhost address; `devflow-jev.py` would be the first script in the repository to do so, independent of which storage location this fork picks. The only existing script found to use the networking module at all connects solely to `127.0.0.1` (R1-arch Q4).

The draft describes the question-set file (`hooks/jev-questions.json`) as governed the same way as an existing prompt-registry file, but R1-arch found the existing prompt-registry schema validates version numbers, content hashes, source SHAs, change classes, and human approvals, none of which exist for the question-set file, which has no schema or validator today — a governance-maturity fact independent of which ledger location this fork picks. R1-arch's reading found the similarity holds only at the level of "both are a JSON file under `hooks/`," not at the level of what machinery validates either one (R1-arch, pipeline table).

An existing file-distribution manifest already copies listed files into adopting projects' local tools directory via a flat list of source/destination/mode rows, currently nine rows, using a schema versioned independently of any individual entry; adding the jev script to it is, per R1-arch's full read of the manifest and its consuming logic, additive regardless of the storage location decided in this fork (R1-arch Q5).

The repository's own minimum-Python-version check compiles every script under the scanned directories, including `memory/`, with a 3.9-floor interpreter; whichever storage mechanism this fork selects, the script that writes to it must avoid language features newer than Python 3.9, a constraint independent of which of the three options is chosen. None of the three options in this fork changes what data is collected or when a human is asked to review anything; the fork only decides which existing subsystem's write-timing and concurrency-safety guarantees the jev ledger inherits, or whether it establishes its own (R1-arch Q4; draft §6; R1-arch full report).

A.description: Create a new directory, `.dev-flow/jev/`, split one file per session, written directly by the jev script itself the moment each call completes. This path does not go through the existing memory subsystem's consolidation step or through the observability run stream at all.
for: This path is available regardless of whether the existing append-only event function turns out to accept a custom event kind, since it never depends on that unresolved question (open item, R1-arch/R3-process shared note). It also means implementation of the jev script itself is not blocked waiting for that separate test to be run and its result interpreted.

A session-per-file layout directly mirrors the existing events-directory design, which was split the same way specifically to prevent concurrent-append corruption during parallel review (devflow-state (b) table; R2-risk B4). Reusing a layout the project has already validated under real concurrent-write conditions is lower-risk than inventing an untested one.

Writing outside the consolidation call graph means implementation is not blocked on whichever answer testing eventually returns about the existing event function's custom-kind support, letting script development proceed independently of that open question. This decouples the jev script's own development timeline from a separate piece of testing work that neither review completed.

Because this path never touches the existing observability schema or the existing event function's internals, it carries no risk of breaking either mechanism's existing behavior for the features that already depend on them. A change confined to a brand-new directory cannot, by construction, introduce a regression in code paths unrelated to jev.
against: It creates a second, independent write-timing model under `.dev-flow/` (write-on-call rather than write-at-checkpoint/session-end), which is not how any other durable artifact in the directory behaves today (devflow-state (b)). Every other durable artifact in the directory commits at the same two moments; this one alone would commit at a third, different moment.

R3-process's review recommends against exactly this path, preferring to extend the existing append-only event function so the memory subsystem keeps a single write-timing model instead of gaining a second one (R3-process §8). The review frames a second write-timing model as added conceptual overhead for anyone later trying to reason about when data becomes durable.

Nothing in the existing consolidation call graph commits this new file into git, so a separate step must be added to the Build-stage wrap-up sequence or the end-of-Build durability check will correctly flag it as uncommitted at feature completion (R1-arch Q3). No comparable step exists for any other file currently written under `.dev-flow/`, all of which are committed through the same single path.

A second write-timing model means anyone reasoning about when `.dev-flow/` durable data becomes committed must now track two different rules instead of one, increasing the surface a future contributor needs to understand correctly. This is a maintainability cost independent of whether the mechanism itself ever malfunctions.

B.description: Extend the observability run contract so stations other than Build can open a run, and write each jev call as an event inside that run stream, reusing the run identifier as the cross-reference key instead of building a second logging mechanism from scratch.
for: Reusing the run identifier as the join key avoids inventing a second cross-referencing scheme; R4-calib's proposed ledger schema itself lists a run-id field specifically so it can directly reuse an existing identifier rather than build a second linking mechanism (R4-calib §1). J4 and J5 already sit downstream of a station whose run lifecycle this fork's other two options do not need to extend at all.

J4, and possibly J5 if its run-lifetime question resolves favorably, already sit inside a station that has run coverage today, so extending the contract benefits at least those integration points without a separate storage mechanism (R1-arch, coupling table). Only J1, J2, and J3 would remain entirely outside this path regardless of how the run-lifetime question resolves.

Observability events already carry a strict, machine-checked schema with defined error codes for unknown fields, which is a stronger existing governance mechanism than either of the other two options currently has (R1-arch Q2). That existing validation would catch a malformed jev event automatically, without any additional validation code being written specifically for jev.

A single unified event stream means every downstream reporting tool that already consumes observability events could, in principle, also see jev events without learning a second file format or location. Any future tooling built against the observability stream would not need a separate integration just to read jev data.
against: J1, J2, and J3 categorically cannot use this path today: the observability hook fail-closes with no run available before the Build stage starts, and the underlying design explicitly does not guess or self-create a run — this is not a schema change away, it is out of scope for three of the six integration points examined in this evaluation (R1-arch, coupling table).

Writing jev's fields exactly as the draft originally described is rejected today by the schema's own forbidden-field list for verifier-role events, so this path requires an actual schema change, not just a new event-type name (R1-arch Q2). A schema change to a file every other event-emitting mechanism also depends on carries review and testing costs beyond jev's own scope.

Whether J5 itself has a live run at the moment its final verdict is signed is unresolved; R1-arch's initial judgment that J5 was clean was withdrawn on a second reading, pending a direct test of when the Stage-7 run is stopped (R1-arch, "J5 run_id timing" section).

Extending a schema used by every other event-emitting mechanism in the repository to accommodate one new integration is a change with a wider blast radius than a change confined to a new, separate directory only jev writes to. Any mistake in that schema change risks affecting event validation for worker, reviewer, and adviser events that have nothing to do with jev.

C.description: Reuse the existing append-only event function with a new event kind (for example "jev") written into the existing events directory, provided direct testing first confirms the function actually accepts custom event kinds; fall back to a jev-specific directory only if that test fails to confirm it.
for: This keeps the memory subsystem's single write-timing model (checkpoint/session-end) intact rather than adding a second one, which is the specific concern R3-process's review raised about a jev-only directory (R3-process §8). It is the only one of the three options that leaves the existing write-timing model completely unchanged.

The existing events store already solves the concurrent-append problem this fork is otherwise at risk of reintroducing, via its one-file-per-session layout (devflow-state (b) table; R2-risk B4). Reusing it means this fork inherits a concurrency guarantee the project has already relied on rather than needing to re-establish one.

The fallback clause means this option does not depend on an untested assumption succeeding; if the existing function cannot take a custom kind, the same outcome as the directory option is reached without having blocked implementation on that open question. This mechanism was originally designed and hardened for a different event kind, and would only be lightly extended rather than newly written.

Because it reuses a mechanism the memory subsystem already exercises on every checkpoint, any bug the existing event function has already had fixed for other event kinds is inherited for free by the jev event kind too. A newly-built, jev-specific writer would not benefit from that same accumulated debugging history.
against: Whether the existing append-only event function accepts a custom event kind, and whether the architecture-guard scripts whitelist specific directories, is explicitly unresolved and still to be tested (open item, R1-arch/R3-process shared note). Choosing this option commits to a design whose central technical premise has not yet been verified against the actual implementation.

Routing through the consolidation function's checkpoint/session-end timing means a jev ledger entry would not be durably committed until the next checkpoint occurs, rather than at the moment each call completes, a behavior change from a call-time-write design (devflow-state (b), consolidation timing). A behavior change of this kind could surprise anyone who assumed, from the draft's original wording, that ledger writes happen at call time.

This is one reviewer's preference, not a unanimous one; R1-arch's and R2-risk's independent reviews confirmed only that J1-J3 cannot reach observability at all, without themselves taking a position for or against a jev-specific namespace versus extending the existing event function (R3-process §8). R1-arch's review, by contrast, took no position for or against this specific option beyond confirming the other two paths' technical constraints.

If the underlying test later shows the existing function cannot accept a custom kind without changes to its own internals, this option's implementation cost converges on option A's anyway, after having spent time on the test itself. In that scenario the fallback clause avoids a dead end, but does not avoid the time already spent discovering it.

forks.title: Do all seven safety guards gate even shadow-mode code
forks.decision: Must all seven safety guards be complete, with negative tests, before any jev-related code runs, including in shadow mode, or can the guard set be split or built incrementally?
facts: The seven guard groups under discussion are: structured evidence-packet truncation with a forced-human-review fallback, fail-closed handling of API errors (401/429/529/timeout/malformed JSON), a dual opt-in gate for data egress (API key plus a per-project file), a per-session ledger file layout, question-set governance via a content hash, anti-fraud controls on feedback/live-mode/question-set tampering, and an auditable record of who authored each gate verdict. Each guard group is examined by at least one of the four independent reviews, though not all four reviews examine all seven.

R2-risk's closing section lists six of these seven guard groups (the seventh, verdict-authorship auditability, was identified in a later review pass) as, in its own words, necessary before any script code is written: "if these six groups are not done, P1 should not even start writing devflow-jev.py" (R2-risk, closing section, translated). The review frames this as the single most load-bearing recommendation in its entire report.

R2-risk's guard B1 targets a shadow-mode-specific risk: because jev is closed-weight with no public tokenizer, a local token-count estimate used to truncate a packet before sending it will not exactly match the API's own limit, so a truncation bug could silently drop a FAIL result from the packet even while shadow mode is only recording, not routing, and the shadow-period sample that resulted would still count toward later graduation math (R2-risk B1).

R2-risk's review argues the guard requirement should extend to shadow-mode calls specifically, not only live-mode calls, since shadow mode still transmits evidence packets to a third-party API and writes ledger rows that become graduation samples discussed in a separate fork; in this framing a guard gap during shadow mode is a live data-handling risk even though no routing decision is at stake yet (R2-risk B1, B5, closing section).

The original 0-draft did not specify any required ordering between building the seven guards and writing the first line of the jev script; the sequencing question itself was raised by R2-risk's adversarial review, not present in the draft's own phased plan, which described only the script's four subcommands without a guard-ordering rule (draft §6; R2-risk, closing section).

The guards differ in what they technically protect: the opt-in egress gate and the truncation guard concern what evidence leaves the machine and whether it is complete; the anti-fraud and per-gate-lock guards concern who may cause an automatic route to actually take effect once live routing exists, a distinction that does not by itself say which guards must precede which code (R2-risk B3(b)/(c), B5).

During shadow mode, the gate's actual sign-off is always the pre-existing fallback behavior; jev's recommendation is recorded but never changes what a human or fallback agent signs during that period, which is the underlying reason several reviewers treat shadow mode as lower routing-risk even while treating it as non-zero data-handling risk (R4-calib §0.2).

Delaying all script-writing until every guard has negative tests delays the point at which any ledger sample, including shadow-only samples, begins to accumulate; sample accumulation toward the thresholds discussed in a separate fork is calendar-bound rather than effort-bound, per R3-process's review, so any delay in the first sample cannot later be made up by working faster (R3-process §4).

One guard's design (verdict-authorship auditability) includes a transitional rule discussed in this evaluation's materials: labels recorded before that specific guard exists are marked as unverified and excluded from later threshold calculations, rather than being disallowed outright, meaning shadow-period activity before that one guard lands is not necessarily wasted, only discounted.

The anti-fraud guard is structurally dependent on the ledger guard and the question-set-governance guard already existing, since its checks operate on ledger entries and hashed question-sets — the seven guards are not seven independent, parallelizable units regardless of which sequencing option is chosen, so even a fully parallel build plan still has an internal ordering among at least three of the seven (R2-risk B3(c), structural dependency).

The anti-fraud guard's design, per R2-risk's review, includes at least two specific sub-clauses each needing its own negative test: treating same-session `ask`-then-`feedback` calls as suspicious, and requiring a persisted, cross-session comparison when a risk-paths list is narrowed rather than only checking whether it changed within a single session (R2-risk B3(a)/(c)).

R2-risk's adversarial review found the draft's original text internally inconsistent about what "live" scope even means: one section defines a global live/shadow mode while another describes graduation as happening gate-by-gate, a contradiction R2-risk flags as needing a per-gate lock design to resolve, independent of this fork's sequencing question. Under the inconsistent global-mode reading, a single gate reaching its threshold would flip every other gate to live at once, even gates that had accumulated no samples of their own (R2-risk B3(b)).

No shadow-mode ledger sample recorded before the fail-closed API-error guard exists has any defined behavior for what a 429, timeout, or 401 response should do; the draft's original text specified only "no key set → no-op," leaving failure-during-a-call entirely undefined, which R2-risk's review treats as a gap large enough to change routing behavior by accident. R2-risk's review notes that during Build-stage parallel review, several candidates could hit a rate limit at once, making this gap more likely to be exercised than a single-call reading might suggest (R2-risk B2, B4).

Building the script first and adding guards incrementally while shadow calls are already occurring means, for whatever period elapses before each guard lands, at least one packet was sent or one ledger row was written without that guard's protection in place — a trade-off inherent to that option's own mechanics, independent of which sequencing choice is ultimately preferred.

None of the seven guards depend on live-mode routing existing; all can, in principle, be built against a jev script that only ever runs in shadow, since shadow mode's routing behavior (always the pre-existing fallback) does not itself require any guard to have first proven itself in production traffic. R2-risk's adversarial review is the only one of the four reviews that proposes a required ordering between guard completion and shadow-mode code at all; R1-arch's, R3-process's, and R4-calib's reviews each discuss individual guards' technical content without independently taking a position on this fork's sequencing question (R4-calib §0.2).

A.description: Require the guards that protect data egress and data correctness — the opt-in gate, structured truncation, fail-closed error handling, the ledger schema, and question-set hashing — before any shadow-mode call, but allow the two guards affecting only live routing to land later, marking earlier samples as unverified and excluding them from later threshold math.
for: This distinguishes what protects the third-party data transfer and the recorded sample itself (relevant from the first shadow call) from what protects live-routing authorization (relevant only once a gate can auto-route), rather than treating all seven guards as a single indivisible unit, a distinction drawn from how R2-risk's review itself describes each guard's function (R2-risk B3(b)/(c), B5). No other option in this fork draws this particular line between the two categories of risk the seven guards separately address.

Marking pre-authorship-guard samples as unverified and excluding them from later threshold math lets calendar-time progress continue during shadow mode without treating unverified samples as valid evidence toward any later graduation decision. This bookkeeping distinction lets calendar-bound progress continue without asserting that unverified evidence is as trustworthy as verified evidence.

It groups the guards by which risk each one addresses (egress/correctness versus live-routing authorization) rather than treating guard completeness as a single yes/no gate applied uniformly to all seven at once. A risk-based grouping is a different organizing principle than a strict yes/no on whether every guard is complete before anything starts.

It gives the project a way to start recording shadow-mode data sooner than requiring all seven guards, while still requiring every guard R2-risk's review calls a precondition for six of the seven to be complete before the first packet leaves the machine. It also means the two guards affecting only live routing can be developed and tested on a separate schedule from the other five.
against: R2-risk's own closing recommendation treats the six guards it names as a single undifferentiated precondition rather than proposing this two-tier split itself; the split described in this option goes beyond what R2-risk's review itself proposed (R2-risk closing section). The split this option proposes is this fork's own construction, not a design R2-risk's review itself put forward.

Splitting the guards into two tiers requires an additional categorization decision — which guards belong in which tier — that neither the original draft nor R2-risk's review specifies ready-made (draft §6; R2-risk closing section). Without a ready-made categorization to draw on, the project would need to justify its own tiering choice independently.

The anti-fraud guard depends on the ledger and question-set guards already existing, so the "protects data correctness" tier is not cleanly separable in practice from guards this option would place in a later tier (R2-risk B3(c), structural dependency). A guard that is supposed to be in an earlier tier but structurally cannot exist without a later-tier guard undermines the tiering itself.

The unverified-sample bookkeeping this option relies on is itself a feature of only one of the seven guards; if that guard is one of the two placed in the later tier, the mechanism this option depends on to make the split safe would not yet exist either.

B.description: Begin writing the jev script immediately and add each of the seven guards incrementally while the script is already running in shadow mode, on the reasoning that shadow mode never changes what a human or fallback agent signs at any gate, regardless of which guards exist yet.
for: Shadow mode's routing outcome is, by definition, never automatic — the actual sign-off stays exactly what it is today regardless of which guards exist yet — so no gate's real decision changes while guards are still being added (R4-calib §0.2). Two of the seven guards R2-risk's review names as most urgent — truncation and fail-closed error handling — would still need to exist early under this option too.

Sample accumulation toward the thresholds discussed in a separate fork is calendar-bound; starting that clock sooner reaches later thresholds sooner, per R3-process's review (R3-process §4). This is the same calendar-bound logic that favors starting any shadow-mode recording as early as the guard situation allows. That same logic applies to whichever of this fork's three options starts recording the soonest, not to this option uniquely.

This is the ordering the original 0-draft's phased plan implicitly assumed, since that plan did not itself specify that all seven guards must precede the first line of script code (draft §8 phase table). The absence of an explicit ordering in the original plan is silence, not an endorsement of building guards afterward.

Building guards incrementally against a running script gives each guard a concrete, already-flowing stream of real packets and ledger rows to test against, rather than requiring every guard to be validated only against synthetic fixtures before any real data exists. Real packets and real ledger rows can surface edge cases synthetic fixtures did not anticipate, at the cost of those edge cases going unguarded until found.
against: R2-risk's adversarial review argues directly against this ordering: without structured truncation and a defined fail-closed behavior for API errors from the first call, a shadow-mode packet could be truncated in a way that hides a FAIL result, or a transient error could silently be treated as pass-through, before the corresponding guard is added (R2-risk B1, B2).

Without the dual opt-in gate from the first call, any machine with the API key present in its shell environment — including machines running other, unrelated projects — would send evidence packets to the third-party API by default; R2-risk's review describes this as the specific failure mode the opt-in guard exists to prevent (R2-risk B5).

R2-risk's adversarial review states its position on six of the seven guards in the strongest terms among the three options in this fork: that script-writing should not begin at all until they exist (R2-risk, closing section). No other option in this fork states its position in comparably strong or unconditional terms.

Every guard added after the first shadow-mode call means every sample recorded before that guard existed carries whatever risk that specific guard was meant to close, and none of those samples can later be retroactively re-protected once they have already been sent or written. That risk compounds with each additional guard still pending, since more unguarded calls occur the longer the guard list remains incomplete.

C.description: Require all seven safety guards — including the two that affect only live routing — to be fully implemented and covered by negative tests before a single line of the jev script is written, so that no shadow-mode call of any kind is ever made without complete protection in place from the start.
for: R2-risk's adversarial review states this position directly for six of the seven guards: that script-writing should not begin at all until they exist, the strongest form of precondition among the three options in this fork (R2-risk, closing section). No other reviewer's language on this question is quoted as directly or as categorically as R2-risk's.

No partially-guarded evidence packet or ledger sample is ever created under this option, which removes the entire category of risk R2-risk's B1, B2, and B5 findings describe (a truncated packet hiding a FAIL, an undefined API-error behavior, or an unintended cross-project data transfer) at its source (R2-risk B1, B2, B5).

It avoids the two-tier bookkeeping option A would require, since no sample of any kind exists before every guard is in place under this option, and it avoids needing to decide which guards belong in an earlier versus later tier at all. Both R1-arch's and R4-calib's reviews describe the anti-fraud guard's dependency on the other two as a structural fact independent of this fork's answer.

It produces a single, simple statement of readiness — all seven guards pass their negative tests — rather than a compound statement that depends on correctly tracking which of two tiers each recorded sample falls under. A single pass/fail readiness check is also easier to verify mechanically than a two-tier check that depends on correctly classifying each guard.
against: This is, among the three options in this fork, the path with the longest expected time before the first shadow-mode ledger sample exists, and sample accumulation toward the thresholds discussed in a separate fork is calendar-bound rather than effort-bound, so any delay in starting it delays every later date on that calendar (R3-process §4).

The anti-fraud guard depends on the ledger and question-set guards being built first, so "all seven complete" is a dependency chain rather than seven parallel tasks finishing at once, extending the time before all seven, not just one, are done (R2-risk B3(c), structural dependency). Neither R1-arch's nor R4-calib's review takes a position on how much that dependency chain should be allowed to lengthen the overall timeline.

R3-process's review, while not addressing guard sequencing directly, found that J1 and J3 do not carry the same shadow-mode egress or ledger risk as J5 and could otherwise begin producing a felt difference for the owner sooner if not tied to the same all-seven-first requirement (R3-process §4).

Because the two live-routing-only guards cannot matter until a gate can actually auto-route, which is itself gated on a separate statistical threshold examined elsewhere in this evaluation, this option requires finishing work whose benefit would not be exercised until well after shadow mode has already been running under either of the other two options.

forks.title: Graduation threshold for the J5 automatic-ship route
forks.decision: What statistical bar must the shadow-period agreement rate clear before the Ship-gate integration point may auto-route low-risk ships without a human signature?
facts: The original 0-draft's proposal was an observed agreement rate of at least 90% across at least 20 samples, presented in the draft's phased plan without an accompanying confidence-interval calculation (draft §8, phase table).

R4-calib's review computed the exact Wilson 95% confidence interval for 18/20 (90% observed) as [69.9%, 97.2%], and the Clopper-Pearson exact interval as [68.3%, 98.8%] — both computed with a Python script using exact binomial arithmetic, cross-checked against an independent second calculation, with one documented bug (a reversed comparison in an initial binary search) found and corrected before the final numbers were reported (R4-calib §3, "computation method and verification").

R4-calib's review computed that a Wilson lower bound of at least 85% with at least 30 samples is, in practice, met only at 30/30 agreements (88.6% lower bound); 29/30 (96.7% observed) produces a lower bound of only 83.3%, which does not clear 85% — so this threshold, expressed as a lower bound, behaves almost like a zero-overturn requirement at that sample size (R4-calib §4).

R4-calib's review computed that if the true agreement rate were 90% and 20 independent samples were drawn, the probability of observing zero overturns in all 20 is approximately 12.2% — meaning a 90%-observed/20-sample result is neither strong evidence of a very high true rate nor backed by a large sample, a point the review makes to argue that point estimates alone are a poor basis for a graduation decision (R4-calib §3).

R4-calib's review computed that excluding a true error rate above 5% with 95% confidence, given zero observed overturns, requires a minimum of 59 samples under a one-sided test (Clopper-Pearson one-sided upper bound 4.95% at n=59); the two-sided version of the same test requires 72 samples (two-sided upper bound 4.99% at n=72), and the review frames the one-sided framing as the one that matches a question about whether the true rate exceeds a ceiling (R4-calib §3).

R4-calib's review states the graduation denominator must be built from jev's recommendation (what jev would have said), not from the gate's actual sign-off, because the actual sign-off is never automatic during shadow mode — using the actual sign-off as the denominator would make shadow-period data, the only unbiased labeling source examined in this evaluation, produce a denominator of zero (R4-calib §2).

R4-calib's review recommends distinguishing labels by their source (human / fresh-context fallback reviewer / owner self-review) and checking graduation math against the human-only subset specifically, because counting a fallback reviewer agent's agreement as equivalent to a human's risks a circular argument — using one model's judgment to certify removing another model's judgment before it (R4-calib §1, §7).

R4-calib's review found that once a gate is live, human review of an automatically-routed case becomes voluntary rather than mandatory, and voluntary review is not randomly distributed (reviewers tend to sample cases that already look suspicious), making any agreement rate computed on live-period data a biased, optimistic estimate unsuitable for re-certifying a threshold already met in shadow (R4-calib §0.2).

R4-calib's review recommends a "freeze, do not reset" behavior for whichever threshold is chosen: a single overturn during live operation immediately suspends new automatic routing until a human reviews that specific case and records either that it counts toward the existing sample or that it represents a genuine regression; the sample counter itself would reset only on a change of model version, question-set hash, or an explicit regression record — not on the freeze event itself (R4-calib §4).

R4-calib's review computed that if the true agreement rate were actually 95%, the probability of seeing at least one overturn in 20 trials is 64.2%, and in 30 trials is 78.5% — meaning even a well-calibrated gate would be expected to trip a naive reset-on-any-overturn rule most of the time, which is the stated reason for recommending freeze rather than reset (R4-calib §4).

This evaluation's own verification of the Wilson formula (matching R4-calib's methodology in §3) confirms: at 30/30 agreements the lower bound is 88.6%; after one overturn (31 samples, 30 agreements) it drops to 83.8%; returning to an 85% lower bound requires accumulating to 34 samples with 33 agreements (85.1%) — three to four additional zero-overturn samples beyond the one that triggered a freeze under an 85%/n≥30 design specifically.

R4-calib's review treats the threshold for this Ship-gate integration point as a separate question from the threshold for a lower-priority Decide-gate integration point examined in a separate fork, arguing the two carry different error costs and should not share one number, since a wrong approval at the earlier gate is still caught by later gates while a wrong approval here is the design's last line of defense (R4-calib §4, distinguishing the two gates).

TypeSafe's own documentation gives no numeric threshold for jev's `confidence` field at all; the only concrete numeric thresholds TypeSafe publishes anywhere are in a guardrails cookbook, and those thresholds apply to the `noul` and `score` fields, not to `confidence`, and are described there as cookbook-specific rather than platform-wide guidance (research-jev-api.md §8).

R4-calib's review recommends that Brier-score and reliability-diagram calibration checks be computed once roughly 20-30 labeled samples exist, but explicitly labels the minimum sample sizes it suggests for those checks as its own engineering rule of thumb, not an official TypeSafe number, and recommends they remain monitoring tools rather than graduation gates themselves (R4-calib §6).

Any threshold examined in this fork applies only when jev's risk-score answer is also low (cosmetic or contained-logic-change risk); the draft's design routes any packet where jev's risk answer is high to mandatory human review regardless of the agreement-rate probability or which threshold is selected. None of the three options in this fork changes what evidence is assembled into the Ship-gate packet or how jev is asked to evaluate it; the fork decides only the statistical bar the resulting shadow-period samples must clear before a human signature can be skipped for low-risk ships (draft §4, J5 row; R4-calib §4).

A.description: Require zero overturns across at least fifty-nine shadow-period samples where jev recommended an automatic route and a human or fresh-context reviewer independently signed the gate, before any automatic routing goes live. This sample size excludes a true error rate above five percent with ninety-five percent one-sided statistical confidence.
for: This is the smallest sample size found to exclude a true error rate above 5% with 95% one-sided confidence given zero observed overturns; the one-sided framing matches a question about whether the true rate exceeds 5%, rather than a two-sided framing that would need 72 samples for the same confidence (R4-calib §3). That exclusion holds regardless of what the true underlying agreement rate turns out to be, which is the point of a confidence-based guarantee.

It removes the ambiguity R4-calib's review found in a 90%-observed/20-sample pairing, where that observed rate is compatible with a true error rate as high as roughly 30% at that sample size (R4-calib §0.1, §3). That statistical fact is the direct basis for this option's choice of exactly fifty-nine as the minimum sample size.

Requiring literally zero overturns removes the need to define an acceptable overturn count at all, unlike a lower-bound formula, which allows some overturns as sample size grows (R4-calib §4 calculation). A reviewer or the project's own report tooling does not need to compute a confidence interval to know whether the bar has been met.

Because the bar is expressed directly as a sample-size requirement rather than as a ratio, it does not require anyone reasoning about the threshold to separately compute a confidence bound from an observed rate before knowing whether it has been met. A separate, single overturn-triggered freeze mechanism, described for a different threshold in this fork, is not part of this option's own definition.
against: R3-process's review estimated, as a projection rather than a measured figure, that a single gate's sample threshold could take on the order of a quarter to a year to reach at the project's historical feature-production pace even at a lower sample count; fifty-nine zero-overturn samples is a larger bar than a thirty-sample alternative, extending that estimated calendar time further (R3-process §4).

Even a genuinely well-calibrated system with a 95% true agreement rate has a 78.5% chance of producing at least one overturn somewhere in 30 trials, per R4-calib's calculation; sustaining zero overturns across nearly double that many samples is a correspondingly higher bar to clear even for a system already performing well (R4-calib §4).

A zero-overturn requirement at n=59 is more conservative than the same zero-overturn-equivalent bar reached at n=30 under a lower-confidence-bound design; the two are different points on the same conservatism-versus-calendar-time spectrum rather than a difference in kind (R4-calib §3, §4). Both numbers exclude the same 5% ceiling at 95% confidence; they differ only in how many zero-overturn samples that exclusion costs.

A single overturn at any point before reaching 59 samples resets progress toward this threshold to zero under a strict zero-overturn reading, unless a separate freeze-and-resume design like the one described for a lower-sample alternative is also adopted for this option. Whether that reset should apply is a design question this option's plain wording does not itself resolve either way.

B.description: Require the Wilson 95% lower confidence bound on the shadow-period agreement rate to reach at least eighty-five percent, with at least thirty labeled samples, before automatic routing may go live; a single overturn during live operation freezes new automatic routing without resetting the accumulated sample count to zero.
for: This pairing is, at n=30, practically equivalent to requiring the first thirty samples to contain zero overturns (30/30 passes at 88.6%; 29/30 fails at 83.3%), giving it nearly the same statistical strength as a stricter option while requiring roughly half as many samples (R4-calib §4).

Writing the threshold as a lower confidence bound rather than a point estimate directly addresses R4-calib's finding that a bare observed-rate number is uninformative at small sample sizes — the lower bound only clears 85% once enough samples exist to support that claim statistically (R4-calib §0.1, §3). R4-calib's review frames the point-estimate weakness as the core reason a confidence-bound formulation is preferable to a bare percentage at small samples.

A freeze-not-reset design built around this threshold preserves accumulated evidence instead of discarding it after a single incident, which R4-calib's review recommends specifically because a well-calibrated system will trip an overturn-triggered reset most of the time (64.2% at n=20, 78.5% at n=30 for a true 95% rate) (R4-calib §4).

Expressing the bar as a formula rather than a fixed sample count means the required sample size can, in principle, shrink if early observed agreement is unusually strong, or grow if it is weaker, rather than being fixed in advance regardless of what the data shows.
against: Recovering from a single freeze under this design is costly: going from a passing 30-sample record (30/30) to 31 samples with one overturn drops the lower bound to 83.8%, and returning to 85% requires accumulating to 34 samples with 33 agreements (85.1%) — three to four additional zero-overturn samples beyond the one that triggered the freeze (verified against R4-calib's §3 methodology).

This threshold is less conservative than a 59-sample zero-overturn requirement; R4-calib's review frames 85%/n≥30 and its zero-overturn equivalence as a smaller sample than the 59 or 72 needed to formally exclude a true error rate above 5% at the same confidence level (R4-calib §3). R4-calib's review states this comparison explicitly, treating the choice between the two sample sizes as a trade-off rather than a strictly dominant option.

The gap between this threshold and a separately-discussed, lower threshold for a related Decide-gate integration point means the design would carry two different graduation bars across the two gates, a choice this fork's number does not by itself justify beyond the two gates' differing error costs (R4-calib §4).

Because the lower-bound formula is less immediately intuitive than a plain sample count, correctly implementing and auditing it requires either trusting a computed value or independently re-deriving the same Wilson-interval arithmetic each time the threshold is checked. An implementer who mis-derives the formula would not necessarily notice the error without independently re-deriving the correct value first.

C.description: Require an observed agreement rate of at least ninety percent across at least twenty labeled shadow-period samples before automatic routing may go live, permitting up to two overturns within the first twenty samples reviewed before the threshold is considered met and routing may begin.
for: This threshold reaches its required sample count sooner in calendar time than the other two options, since it requires the fewest samples of the three, and sample accumulation runs on calendar time rather than engineering effort per R3-process's review (R3-process §4). Twenty samples at a typical feature-production pace is reached well before either of the other two options' larger sample requirements.

It is the threshold the original 0-draft proposed before the four independent reviews examined it, reflecting an initial judgment about what bar felt adequate before a dedicated statistical analysis (draft §8, phase table). That original judgment predates the statistical analysis in R4-calib's review, which found the underlying pairing did not hold up numerically.

Twenty samples is enough to compute a Brier score as a rough directional signal per R4-calib's review, even though that review recommends a larger sample before treating such a score as stable (R4-calib §6). A rough directional Brier score is still more information than no calibration signal at all, even if not yet statistically stable.

A plain observed-rate threshold is the simplest of the three to state and check by hand, requiring only a count of agreements and overturns rather than a confidence-interval calculation or a fixed large sample target. Simplicity here is a genuine advantage independent of whether the resulting bar turns out to be statistically adequate.
against: R4-calib's review computed the exact 95% confidence interval for this scenario (18/20, 90% observed) as [69.9%, 97.2%] Wilson, or [68.3%, 98.8%] Clopper-Pearson — meaning this observed rate at this sample size is statistically compatible with a true error rate as high as roughly 30%, which the review states directly conflicts with a 5% error-rate exclusion goal (R4-calib §0.1, §3). That compatibility with a materially higher true error rate is the central numerical finding R4-calib's review reports about this pairing.

R4-calib's review computed that a 90%-with-20-samples observation is, at a true 90% rate, only a roughly one-in-eight event (about 12.2% probability) — neither the strong evidence a much larger sample would provide nor the strong evidence a zero-overturn result would provide (R4-calib §3). Both figures come from the same underlying binomial calculation R4-calib's review applied consistently across every threshold examined in this fork.

A 75%-lower-bound design at the same n=20 sample size (one candidate threshold discussed for a related, lower-priority gate in a separate fork) would in practice require 19/20 agreements to pass — a stricter practical bar than this option's plain 90%-observed-rate requirement at the same sample size once both are expressed as confidence-bound calculations (R4-calib §4).

Because this option accepts up to two overturns within the first twenty samples, it reaches its threshold under a wider range of possible early outcomes than a design that would freeze or reset on the first overturn, which also means it tolerates more early error before pausing to reassess.

forks.title: What to do with automatic approval at the Decide gate
forks.decision: Should automatic approval at the Decide gate be built at all, and if so, on what timeline relative to the Ship-gate automatic-routing work?
facts: This integration point (automatic approval at the Decide gate) does not correspond to any of the seven sentences the owner used to describe his preferred flow; R3-process's requirement-mapping table explicitly lists it as one of two integration points, out of six examined across the evaluation, that map onto none of those sentences (R3-process §1, closing note).

R3-process's review argues the Ship-gate integration point's evidence packet is qualitatively different from this one's: the Ship-gate packet draws on Final Fresh Run, Evidence Gauntlet results, the two-axis review, and Operational Walkthrough, while this integration point's packet is a plan-comparison table and a list of Owner Calls, which the review describes as weighted more heavily toward subjective judgment than toward mechanically-produced evidence (R3-process §1, closing note).

This integration point and the Ship-gate integration point are described in the draft as requiring the same underlying contract change — rewriting the reviewer-selection clause and the gate-consistency hook — making this one comparatively cheap to add once that contract change has already landed for the other, though each would still need to accumulate its own separate graduation sample before either could actually auto-route anything (draft §7 table). Neither integration point can be built without touching whichever of these files the other has not already modified, so the marginal cost only applies to whichever is built second.

R1-arch's full read of the gate-consistency script found the reviewer-selection clause is synchronized across five files, plus a separate ten-file family covering how a gate verdict may be written at all, none of which either this integration point or the Ship-gate one can avoid touching if its automatic path is built, regardless of the order in which the two are built (R1-arch, "contract synchronization" section).

At the Decide gate, every Owner Call must still be answered by the project owner personally under the project's stated verification laws; the draft's design for this integration point uses jev's output only to order and pre-fill a suggested answer for each Owner Call, with the owner confirming or overriding each one individually — jev is never permitted to answer an Owner Call itself under any option in this fork (draft §4 row; devflow-state (a), Owner Call row).

R3-process's review recommends, if this integration point is built at all, sequencing it after the Ship-gate one rather than alongside it, reasoning that the Ship gate is a station the owner experiences as a heavier stop point today, while this gate's felt friction for the owner is unconfirmed and only inferred from packet composition rather than measured (R3-process §1, closing note, explicitly flagged there as inference not measurement).

A wrong automatic approval at the Decide gate sends an incorrect direction into the Spec and Build stations, where it is caught later at a downstream gate but only after work has already been spent following that direction — a distinct error mode from a wrong automatic approval at the Ship gate, which the draft frames as generally lower-cost by comparison since there is no further downstream gate to catch it (draft §4 row; R4-calib §4, comparing the two gates' error costs).

Building this integration point and the Ship-gate one in the same contract-change pass would start both gates' graduation clocks at roughly the same time, rather than this gate's clock beginning only once the other has already reached live status on its own; either way, each gate's own samples must still accumulate separately (structural consequence of building the two together versus sequentially).

R4-calib's review assigns this integration point its own, separately lower, statistical bar if it is built at all — a 75% Wilson lower bound at n≥20 — explicitly distinguishing it from the Ship-gate integration point's 85%/n≥30 bar on the grounds that a wrong approval here is still caught downstream, lowering the cost of an error relative to a Ship-gate error (R4-calib §4).

R4-calib's review notes that at n=20, a 75% Wilson lower bound is in practice reached at 19/20 observed agreement (95%), a stricter bar in practice than a flat 75% figure suggests, since 18/20 (90% observed) only clears a lower bound of 69.9%, well short of 75% (R4-calib §4). A stricter-in-practice bar of this kind is a direct numerical consequence of the same Wilson-interval arithmetic used for the Ship-gate integration point's threshold, not a separately chosen number.

Contract changes to the reviewer-selection clause require opening the project's own Decide-station process and a design-decision record, per the draft's own classification of any automatic-routing gate change as requiring that process, regardless of which of this fork's three options is chosen (draft §7 table, bottom row).

Both this integration point's and the Ship-gate integration point's automatic-routing proposals are independently classified in the draft as requiring the project's own Decide-station process and a design-decision record before implementation, a classification that does not itself depend on which of the two is built first or whether both are built together (draft §7 table, bottom row).

Dropping this integration point entirely removes any future need to give the Decide gate its own separate graduation ledger, threshold, or freeze/reset design, since none of those exist for an integration point that is never built (draft §7 table; R4-calib §4, noting the two gates should not share one threshold only if both are built).

None of this fork's three options changes Owner Call handling at the Decide gate; in every option, jev's role there (where implemented at all) is limited to ordering and pre-filling suggested answers, with the owner retaining sole authority to answer each Owner Call, consistent with the project's stated rule that an agent may never answer on the owner's behalf (draft §4 row; devflow-state (a), Owner Call row).

R3-process's review is the only one of the four reviews that takes a position on this integration point's priority relative to the Ship-gate one; R1-arch's review addresses it only from a contract-coupling perspective (how many files must change) and R4-calib's review addresses it only from a statistical-threshold perspective, neither endorsing nor opposing building it at all (R1-arch "contract synchronization" section; R4-calib §4).

A.description: Do not build automatic approval at the Decide gate. Keep the gate exactly as it is today, with every Owner Call answered by the project owner and every verdict signed through the existing reviewer-selection chain, and allocate no contract-change or ledger work to this integration point.
for: R3-process's requirement-mapping review found this integration point does not correspond to any sentence in the owner's own description of his preferred flow, unlike the other integration points examined in this evaluation, which each map to something the owner explicitly said (R3-process §1, closing note). R3-process's review is explicit that this absence is a finding about the owner's own words, not an assumption about what he might want.

It avoids opening the reviewer-selection contract change and its associated five-file and ten-file synchronization work for an integration point that, per R3-process's review, has a comparatively weaker evidence packet than the packet available at the Ship gate (R1-arch, R3-process §1). The review draws this distinction from the specific kinds of evidence each gate's packet actually contains, not from the number of files each touches.

It removes the need for a separate graduation ledger, threshold, and freeze/reset design at the Decide gate altogether, since an integration point that is never built accumulates no samples and needs no threshold (R4-calib §4). No separate report format, freeze/reset rule, or circuit-breaker state needs to be specified for a gate that does not exist.

It leaves no automatic-routing surface at the Decide gate for the anti-fraud and per-gate-lock guards examined in a separate fork to protect, simplifying what those guards need to cover to only the Ship gate and, if built, no other automatic-routing gate.
against: The draft's original framing treats this integration point as nearly free to add once the Ship-gate contract change already exists, since both require the same reviewer-selection rewrite; not building it forgoes that marginal reuse entirely (draft §7 table). That reuse is forgone specifically for the marginal, already-amortized portion of the contract-change cost, not for the whole cost.

A wrong Decide-gate direction is caught later at downstream gates under every option including this one, since approving it either way does not remove those downstream checks; dropping this integration point removes a potential efficiency gain (fewer manual approvals) without a countervailing safety cost identified in this fork's facts (draft §4 row).
