Neither R1-arch's nor R4-calib's review takes a position against building this integration point on safety or feasibility grounds specifically; the case against it in this fork's facts rests on R3-process's priority argument alone, not a majority or technical-infeasibility finding (R1-arch; R4-calib §4; R3-process §1). Both reviews examined this integration point from a narrower angle than R3-process's review, which is the only one to weigh it against the other gate directly.

If a later, currently-unstated need for this integration point emerges, this option would require reopening the contract-change process from scratch rather than building on an already-validated rewrite, unlike an option that builds it now alongside or after the Ship gate. That reopening cost is the same size regardless of how much time has passed since this option was first chosen.

B.description: Build this integration point's automatic approval in the same contract-change pass as the Ship-gate integration point's automatic approval, reusing the same reviewer-selection rewrite and gate-consistency hook update for both gates at once, and let each gate accumulate and graduate against its own separate ledger threshold afterward, independently of the other.
for: Both integration points already require the same underlying contract change — the reviewer-selection clause rewrite and gate-consistency hook update — so doing both in one pass avoids opening and re-verifying that same five-file-plus-ten-file synchronization twice (draft §7 table; R1-arch, file count). That reuse benefit is the same regardless of which of the two gates is described as built "first" within the shared pass.

Each gate still graduates against its own separately-tracked ledger and threshold under this option, so building the contract change together does not, by itself, let a sample from one gate count toward the other's threshold (R4-calib §4, distinguishing the two gates' thresholds). Independent tracking is what lets each gate's own report correctly state whether it, specifically, has met its own bar.

It avoids a second, later contract-change review cycle and a second design-decision record for this integration point if the project later decides to build it anyway, since both would already be covered by the first pass (draft §7 table, bottom row). That reuse benefit does not depend on which of the two gates the project later decides to prioritize operationally.

Building both gates' automatic-routing mechanics against the same anti-fraud and per-gate-lock guard implementation in one pass means any bug found and fixed in that shared mechanism during review benefits both gates immediately, rather than being found once and then separately re-verified for a second gate later.
against: R3-process's review explicitly recommends against this ordering, arguing the Ship gate's evidence packet and felt owner friction both make it the higher-priority gate, and that this integration point should wait until the Decide gate is independently shown to be a comparable pain point (R3-process §1, closing note).

Building both means the single contract-change review must reason about two automatic-routing gates' worth of downstream consequences at once, rather than validating the reviewer-selection rewrite against one gate's real-world graduation data before extending it to a second (draft §7 table). R4-calib's review frames the two gates' differing error costs as a reason to keep their statistical machinery separate even when built together.

R4-calib's review treats the two gates as needing different, separately-justified statistical bars precisely because their error costs differ; building the contract change for both at once does not remove the need to keep their graduation math and freeze/reset behavior fully separate, and increases the surface reviewed in a single pass (R4-calib §4).

If the shared contract change later needs a correction after real-world use of the Ship gate reveals a problem, that correction affects an already-built Decide-gate mechanism too, whereas a strictly sequential build would only need to revisit the gate already reached at that point. A correction of this kind is more likely the newer and less-exercised of the two gates' mechanism is, which is this integration point under this option.

C.description: Keep this integration point in scope, but sequence it strictly after the Ship-gate integration point's automatic approval has already reached live status, and give it its own, lower statistical bar — a Wilson lower bound of at least seventy-five percent with at least twenty labeled samples.
for: This is the ordering R3-process's review recommends, on the grounds that the Ship gate's packet is stronger and its owner-felt friction is established, while this gate's friction is only inferred; sequencing it after the Ship gate means the contract-change and reviewer-selection rewrite are validated against real graduation data from one gate before being extended to a second (R3-process §1, closing note).

R4-calib's review supplies a specific, lower bar for this integration point (75% lower bound, n≥20) distinct from the Ship gate's (85%, n≥30), reflecting that a wrong approval here is caught downstream, which the review treats as a lower error cost than a wrong Ship-gate approval (R4-calib §4).

Because the same contract change is needed for both gates, sequencing this one after the other rather than dropping it entirely still lets the project reuse the already-validated reviewer-selection rewrite rather than repeating that review from scratch (draft §7 table). That reuse benefit is smaller than building the two together, since the reviewer for this pass sees only one gate's consequences at a time.

Waiting for the Ship gate to reach live status first means any operational lessons learned from running an automatic-routing gate for the first time — including how the freeze/reset behavior examined elsewhere in this evaluation performs in practice — are available before the same mechanism is extended to a second gate.
against: It defers any benefit from this integration point until after the Ship-gate one has already independently reached live status, which R3-process's own calendar-time estimate suggests could be on the order of a quarter to a year away, meaning this gate's own graduation clock does not even start until that point (R3-process §4, flagged as an estimate).

At n=20, R4-calib's review notes the 75% lower-bound bar is in practice reached only at 19/20 observed agreement, a stricter practical bar than a flat 75%-sounding number suggests, and one more sample-dependent threshold the project must separately monitor and report on (R4-calib §4). R4-calib's review presents this as a general property of the Wilson-bound formula, not something specific to this particular gate.

It commits to eventually building this integration point and its associated contract change, ledger, and threshold machinery, rather than deciding, as another option would, that the effort is not justified by anything the owner has stated wanting (R3-process §1, closing note). R3-process's review is explicit that this is the one integration point among six examined that the owner never mentioned.

Sequencing this gate strictly after the other means its own graduation clock cannot start any earlier than the Ship gate's does, compounding whatever calendar-time estimate applies to the Ship gate with an additional, separate accumulation period specific to this gate. That compounding is a direct consequence of the strict "after" ordering this option specifies, rather than a looser "eventually" ordering.

forks.title: When to make the e2e verification layer mandatory
forks.decision: Should the e2e verification mandatory-check be finished before J5 shadow-mode sampling begins, or can sampling start first with the mismatch handled some other way?
facts: R4-calib's proposed ledger schema keys agreement-rate grouping by a triple — gate, question-set content hash, and resolved model version — deliberately not including evidence-packet content or shape as a grouping dimension (R4-calib §1).

R4-calib's review describes the criteria-hash-based reset (any change to the question-set text creates a new sample group automatically) as a deliberate, conservative design choice, and states that if this cost is later found too high, its preferred fix is to freeze the question-set text as a stable contract rather than to keep expanding what counts as a grouping dimension. The review frames even a spelling correction to a question's wording as something that could, in principle, change jev's answer distribution, which is why it treats any text change as grounds for a fresh sample group rather than trying to judge which changes are "meaningful" (R4-calib §5).

If evidence packets begin including an e2e summary partway through a shadow-mode sampling period, a fixed sample threshold examined in a separate fork would contain a mix of two different packet shapes — with and without an e2e summary — unless something accounts for that change; the grouping key described above does not track packet shape and so would not separate them automatically.

The e2e mandatory-check itself is described as a medium-sized, self-contained change to an existing spec-gate script and its templates, and does not depend on jev, the ledger, or any of the seven safety guards examined in a separate fork, meaning it could in principle be built on a completely independent timeline from the rest of the jev integration (draft §4.1).

Today, the existing spec-gate script's checks do not require any Verification Profile to include an e2e layer; a feature can declare its Required layers as "none" with a reason and still pass the Spec gate, meaning e2e's status as a Required layer is currently declarative rather than mechanically enforced (R3-process §1, row on automated e2e).

At least one reviewer (R3-process) recommends completing the e2e mandatory-check before J5 shadow-mode sampling begins, listing it as one of two low-cost items worth doing early, specifically to avoid mixing evidence-packet shapes inside one sample pool (R3-process §5).

The draft frames e2e's promotion to a Required layer as directly answering the owner's own stated preference for automatic verification after execution, translating that preference into a Verification Profile layer rather than into a jev-judged question, meaning the check's existence does not itself depend on any of this fork's three options (draft §2 table; §4.1).

If shadow sampling begins before the e2e check exists, and the sample pool is later reset manually once e2e summaries begin appearing, whatever samples had accumulated up to that point are discarded, restarting the calendar-bound accumulation process described in a separate fork from zero, with no partial credit for the discarded samples.

The e2e check, as described in the 0-draft, adds one new assertion: that any feature involving interactive or external-API behavior must declare a single entry-point command for its e2e layer in the Verification Profile, or explicitly state "none" with a reason; Final Fresh Run then executes it, bound to the frozen commit SHA under review, and the Evidence Gauntlet verifies it actually ran rather than only being declared in the profile text (draft §4.1).

The original 0-draft scoped e2e's promotion to a Required layer as a template-only, purely additive change, without proposing any mechanical check to enforce that a project actually declares an e2e entry-point command; the mechanical assertion itself is a distinct design decision layered on top of that original template change (draft §4.1, §7 table).

None of dev-flow's own CI or self-test suites run an actual end-to-end test against a real application, because dev-flow is a methodology and tooling repository without its own user interface; the e2e layer discussed in this fork exists entirely within adopting projects' own Verification Profiles, not within dev-flow's own test suite (devflow-state, "explicitly absent" section).

Whichever option this fork selects, the underlying e2e check itself — the assertion requiring a declared entry-point command or an explicit waiver — is the same medium-sized, jev-independent change; the three options differ only in whether J5 shadow-mode sampling is required to wait for it, and if not, how a resulting packet-shape mismatch is handled (draft §4.1).

R2-risk's adversarial review does not address e2e timing at all; its recommendations focus on the seven safety guards examined in a separate fork and evidence-packet truncation, and do not mention the e2e check anywhere in its text.

R1-arch's review, in the course of examining a different question (contract synchronization), separately confirmed that an existing file-mapping check turns red as soon as any new script file is added anywhere in the scanned directories, including a script for the e2e check or for jev itself, regardless of this fork's timing choice — meaning either the e2e work or the jev work, whichever lands first, triggers that same bookkeeping requirement first (R1-arch, file-map section).

Evidence Gauntlet, the existing script that checks whether declared Verification Profile layers actually ran, is described as already capable of checking an e2e layer's pass/fail status once one is declared; the gap this fork addresses is specifically that nothing today forces a project to declare one in the first place, not that the checking mechanism itself is missing. None of the three options in this fork change what the e2e check itself asserts once it exists; they differ only in whether J5 shadow-mode sampling is required to wait for it, and if not, how the resulting packet-shape mismatch this fork's facts describe is handled (devflow-state (c), Evidence Gauntlet row; R3-process §1).

A.description: Start J5 shadow-mode recording with whatever evidence already exists, without waiting for the e2e mandatory-check to be built at all. Add the e2e check later, and when it lands, manually discard the J5 sample pool accumulated up to that point and restart counting from zero.
for: It lets J5 shadow sampling begin as soon as the seven safety guards examined in a separate fork are ready, without an additional wait for a separate, jev-independent piece of work to also finish first (draft §4.1, describing e2e as independent of jev). That independence from guard-completion timing is a property this option shares only with the option that also does not wait for the e2e check.

Sample accumulation toward the thresholds examined in a separate fork is calendar-bound, so starting the clock immediately, even knowing a manual reset may later be needed, starts progress sooner than waiting for the e2e check first (R3-process §4, flagged as an estimate). R3-process's review frames calendar-bound accumulation as the single largest lever available for reaching any of this evaluation's thresholds sooner. No engineering time is spent up front deciding how to classify or track packet shape under this option, unlike the alternative that extends the grouping key.

A manual reset is an explicit, visible action a person takes and records, rather than an automatic one a script performs silently, which keeps the decision to discard samples in front of a human rather than embedded in code. Under the other two options, no comparable human-visible checkpoint marks the moment the packet shape changed. No comparable record of exactly when the switch happened exists under either of the other two options in this fork.

If the e2e check turns out to take longer to build than expected, this option's shadow-mode samples continue accumulating in the meantime rather than sitting idle waiting for an unrelated piece of engineering work to finish first. Progress made during that period is not wasted even though it will later be discarded, since it still validates the shared pipeline.
against: A manually-triggered reset depends on a person noticing that packet shape changed and remembering to execute the reset; nothing in this option's own mechanics forces that notice to happen at the correct moment, unlike a check that runs automatically before sampling starts. R3-process's review, by contrast, recommends finishing the check first specifically to avoid ever needing this kind of visible, manual correction.

At least one reviewer (R3-process) recommends the opposite ordering — finishing the e2e check before shadow sampling starts — listing it as one of two low-cost items worth doing early (R3-process §5). No other reviewer's materials propose the opposite ordering as explicitly as R3-process's review does.

Whatever samples accumulate before the manual reset are discarded entirely once e2e summaries begin appearing, meaning any calendar-time progress made in the interim toward the thresholds examined in a separate fork is lost at the moment of reset rather than preserved. No comparable loss of accumulated progress occurs under either of the other two options in this fork.

Because the reset depends on a person's judgment about when the packet shape has changed enough to matter, two different people could reasonably disagree about the right moment to reset, introducing a subjective judgment call that neither of the other two options requires. Two different people reasonably applying the same judgment call could reach different conclusions about exactly when to reset, which is itself a source of inconsistency.

B.description: Start J5 shadow-mode recording without waiting for the e2e check, and add evidence-packet shape as a fourth dimension to the ledger's existing grouping key, so that samples recorded before and after the e2e summary begins appearing are automatically separated into different groups rather than requiring a manual reset.
for: It removes the need for a human to notice, decide, and manually execute a sample-pool reset at the moment e2e summaries begin appearing, replacing that manual step with an automatic mechanical separation. That automatic behavior would apply uniformly the first time a shape change occurs and every time thereafter.

It lets J5 shadow sampling begin immediately, on the same timeline as starting without the e2e check, while avoiding the requirement that accumulated samples be discarded rather than automatically re-grouped. Both options that do not wait for the e2e check share this same immediate-start property. That immediacy property is shared only with the option that also begins recording before the e2e check is finished.

The ledger schema already has room for additional grouping dimensions in principle, since the existing key (gate, question-set hash, resolved model version) is itself a tuple that could be extended with a fourth element describing packet shape (R4-calib §1, describing the current three-element key). That schema-extension property is unique to this option among the three examined in this fork.

Once implemented, this mechanism would also automatically handle any future evidence-packet shape change beyond just the e2e summary, without needing a new manual-reset decision each time the packet's contents change again later. No comparable future-proofing exists under either of the other two options, both of which handle only this one known shape change.
against: R4-calib's review describes the current three-element grouping key as a deliberate, conservative design choice specifically because packet-content changes are numerous and often incidental, and states its own preferred fix for a costly reset is to freeze the question-set text as a stable contract, not to keep expanding the grouping key (R4-calib §5). R4-calib's review frames this preference as applying to any grouping-key extension, not only to the specific one this option proposes.

Adding evidence-packet shape as a grouping dimension increases the schema's dimensionality permanently, for a change that, once it exists, does not change again — the added dimension continues to apply to every future evidence-packet change, not only this one. A grouping key that keeps growing is harder to reason about than one whose dimensions stay fixed over the life of the design.

Adding a dimension to the grouping key means samples recorded before e2e summaries existed accumulate in a permanently smaller group that can never merge with later samples, a different, permanent form of the same fragmentation problem a one-time manual reset causes once. R4-calib's review does not itself propose this specific extension as a solution to the mismatch this fork's facts describe.

Defining what counts as a distinct "packet shape" for grouping purposes is itself a new design decision this option requires that neither of the other two options needs, since a manual reset or a wait-first approach does not need packet shape formally classified into groups at all.

C.description: Finish building the e2e mandatory-check — the assertion requiring a declared entry-point command or an explicit written waiver — before J5 shadow-mode recording begins at all, so that every sample later collected in the J5 sample pool shares exactly the same evidence-packet shape from the very first sample onward, with no exceptions.
for: Finishing the e2e check before any J5 shadow sample is recorded means every sample in the pool shares one packet shape by construction, without needing either a manual reset step or a grouping-key extension to handle a shape change after the fact. No manual judgment call and no additional schema dimension are needed under this option, unlike either of the other two.

At least one reviewer (R3-process) independently recommends this ordering, listing the e2e check as one of two low-cost items worth finishing early, before shadow-mode sampling begins (R3-process §5). That recommendation is made independently of R4-calib's grouping-key analysis, arriving at the same conclusion from a different angle.

It avoids both of the other two options' downsides at once: no manual reset is ever needed and no permanent grouping-key fragmentation is introduced, because every J5 sample shares one packet shape from the start. No other option in this fork avoids both costs simultaneously; each of the other two avoids only one.

Because the check is described as a medium-sized, self-contained, jev-independent piece of work, its completion date does not depend on any of the seven safety guards examined in a separate fork, so it can, in principle, be scheduled in parallel with guard work rather than only after it.
against: It delays the start of J5 shadow-mode sample accumulation by however long the e2e check itself takes to build (a self-described medium-sized change), and that accumulation is calendar-bound rather than effort-bound, so any delay in starting it delays every later threshold date examined in a separate fork (draft §4.1; R3-process §4).

The e2e check is, by the draft's own account, entirely independent of jev and the seven safety guards examined in a separate fork; requiring it to finish first ties two otherwise-unrelated pieces of engineering work together on the critical path to J5's first sample (draft §4.1). That independence cuts both ways: delays on one do not delay the other, but neither can either timeline pull the other forward.

The existing spec-gate script today accepts "none" with a reason as a valid Required-layer declaration, so a feature can already pass the Spec gate without a true e2e layer; this option adds a stricter mechanical requirement than the gate demands today, which is itself a scope increase to what must be delivered before J5 shadow can start (R3-process §1). Today's permissive default was presumably chosen for some reason by the project, though neither the draft nor any of the four reviews states what that reason was. Whichever reason motivated the permissive default, this option overrides it specifically for features feeding into the J5 sample pool.

If the e2e check's own build takes longer than expected, every downstream date this fork's facts describe as calendar-bound — including the graduation thresholds examined in a separate fork — shifts later by the same amount, with no partial shadow-mode data collected in the meantime to offset it.

forks.title: How human feedback labels are collected during shadow mode
forks.decision: What mechanism, if any, collects the human feedback labels that jev's shadow-period recommendations are compared against?
facts: The Decide, Spec, and Ship gates already produce a signed frontmatter verdict plus a reviewers field recording who signed, through the existing reviewer-selection chain, independent of whether jev is integrated at all (devflow-state (a), gate rows).

During shadow mode, the gate's actual sign-off is always the pre-existing fallback behavior — a human or fallback agent signs the gate exactly as they do today — so the frontmatter verdict already produced for every gated feature can, in principle, be paired against jev's recorded recommendation for the same gate and slug without asking anyone an additional question (R4-calib §0.2; R3-process §3).

R3-process's review states that the draft's original design — a standalone feedback command with no described prompt location, timing, or default behavior — assumes the owner will remember to run it unprompted, which the review calls the single largest point-of-failure risk in the whole roadmap, since if nobody runs it, the ledger never accumulates enough samples for any threshold examined in a separate fork to be reached. The review frames this as the one risk capable of quietly stalling the entire jev integration without any error message or visible failure ever appearing (R3-process §3).

R4-calib's review identifies a distinct risk in any design that shows jev's recommendation to a human before asking for their independent judgment: this ordering produces an anchoring effect that systematically inflates the resulting agreement rate, and recommends that the human or fallback agent give an independent answer first, with jev's answer shown only afterward (R4-calib §2).

One possible design for a post-graduation feedback mechanism batches short yes/no questions at most once per week, surfaced at a touchpoint already visited during normal use, with an unanswered prompt recorded as a neutral state excluded from the agreement-rate denominator rather than counted as agreement (this is the mechanism described in one of this fork's options below).

Once a gate reaches live status, an automatically-routed case is, by design, no longer reviewed by a human by default; R4-calib's review states that voluntary review of such cases is not randomly distributed (people tend to spot-check cases that already look suspicious), making any agreement rate computed purely from voluntary live-period reviews a biased, optimistic estimate. This is why R4-calib's review treats shadow-period data, where every case is still reviewed as a matter of routine, as the only sound basis for the threshold calculations examined in a separate fork (R4-calib §0.2, §5).

R4-calib's review recommends a mandatory minimum spot-check rate during live operation — 10 to 20 percent of automatically-routed cases per gate — specifically to counteract the label-staleness problem described above, since without a floor, the agreement rate would increasingly reflect only the subset of cases someone happened to double-check (R4-calib §5).

R4-calib's proposed report format includes a `labeled_fraction` metric — the proportion of automatically-routed cases in a trailing window that actually received a human or fallback-agent label — specifically so a declining labeling rate during live operation is visible rather than silently absorbed into the agreement-rate calculation. R2-risk's adversarial review separately raises the same underlying concern from a different angle: a feedback request delivered through a channel the owner does not routinely check risks a response rate approaching zero regardless of how the request is worded (R4-calib §7; R2-risk M2).

R4-calib's proposed ledger schema distinguishes labels by source — human, fresh-context fallback reviewer, owner self-review, or unverified/uncertain origin — and recommends that graduation math be checked against the human-only subset specifically, to avoid one model's agreement being used to certify removing another model's human-equivalent review (R4-calib §1, §7).

One guard's design (verdict-authorship auditability), discussed in this evaluation's materials, marks labels recorded before it exists as unverified and excludes them from the graduation-threshold denominator entirely, regardless of which feedback-collection design this fork selects.

A design that asks a separate, additional question at the end of every feature, rather than reusing the gate's existing frontmatter verdict, adds one guaranteed touchpoint per feature to the owner's workflow, in a project whose owner is otherwise described, in his own stated preferences, as wanting fewer such touchpoints over time (draft §2, owner's stated preferences table).

A design that collects no labels at all and graduates purely on jev's own reported confidence value has no independent way to verify that confidence is actually calibrated for this specific use case, since TypeSafe's own documentation states calibration is measured only across groups of predictions in aggregate and does not certify any individual model's confidence value as accurate for a new domain without its own validation data (research-jev.md §7, quoting TypeSafe's documentation verbatim).

jev's `confidence` field carries no official numeric threshold guidance from TypeSafe at all; the only concrete numeric thresholds TypeSafe publishes anywhere are in a guardrails cookbook, and those thresholds apply to the `noul` and `score` fields, not to `confidence` (research-jev-api.md §8).

An auto-pairing mechanism that reuses the existing frontmatter verdict depends on that verdict being trustworthy as genuinely human-or-fallback-agent-authored; before the verdict-authorship guard discussed above exists, any such auto-paired label would be marked unverified per the rule described in that guard's design.

Every threshold design examined elsewhere in this evaluation is built around comparing jev's recommendation to an independent human-or-fallback-agent label; a design that collects no labels removes the only data source that comparison depends on, which none of the four reviews propose as sufficient on its own. None of this fork's three options change what evidence jev is shown or what questions it is asked at any gate; the fork decides only how, if at all, an independent human or fallback-agent judgment is collected to compare against jev's recommendation after the fact (R4-calib §1-§4, entire ledger-and-threshold design; draft §6).

A.description: At the end of every feature, regardless of gate mode, present a dedicated feedback prompt asking whether jev's recommendation at each gate was correct, in addition to whatever frontmatter verdict the gate itself already produced, and record the answer as the ledger's human-feedback label for that gate every time.
for: It produces a label from an explicit, deliberate act every time, rather than relying on an inference drawn from a frontmatter verdict recorded for an unrelated purpose (draft §6, original feedback-command design). That deliberateness also makes it straightforward to distinguish a genuine "no opinion" response from a person who has not yet been asked at all.

A dedicated prompt can be worded to ask specifically about jev's recommendation, rather than reusing a verdict field whose wording and purpose were designed for a different question (the gate's own pass/hold/rework decision, not an opinion about jev). The gate's own verdict field was never designed with jev's existence in mind, since it predates any jev integration entirely.

It works identically in shadow and live modes without needing two different collection designs, unlike an approach that relies on a frontmatter verdict that stops being paired with a mandatory human review once a gate goes live (R4-calib §0.2, describing that behavior difference). That difference in wording could matter if a human agreed with the overall gate outcome for reasons unrelated to jev's specific recommendation.

Because the prompt is asked freshly every time rather than inferred from an existing field, it can in principle also capture cases where the human agreed with the gate's overall outcome but would have disagreed with jev's specific recommendation, a distinction an inferred label cannot make. Neither of the other two options in this fork produces a label capable of drawing that particular distinction.
against: R3-process's review identifies this exact design — a standalone prompt with no described location, timing, or default behavior — as the single largest failure risk in the whole roadmap, because it depends entirely on the owner remembering to answer it, in a workflow the owner has otherwise described wanting to interrupt him less over time (R3-process §3). No comparable single point of failure exists under either of the other two options, both of which reduce or remove the dependence on an unprompted, remembered action.

It adds one guaranteed additional touchpoint per feature beyond what exists today, when the existing frontmatter verdict already provides an equivalent label for free during shadow mode without asking anything new (R3-process §3, contrasting with an auto-pairing alternative). That additional touchpoint recurs on every feature indefinitely, not only during an initial rollout period.

Nothing in this option's description addresses the ordering-and-anchoring concern raised elsewhere in this evaluation — whether jev's recommendation is shown before or after the human's independent answer — leaving that risk unresolved unless separately specified (R4-calib §2). Anchoring risk of this kind does not disappear on its own; it has to be designed against explicitly.

Because every feature produces a prompt regardless of mode, the total number of times the owner is asked something grows in direct proportion to how many features ship, rather than staying flat or shrinking as the project's own stated goal of reducing human-in-the-loop review over time would suggest (draft §2, owner's stated preferences table).

B.description: During shadow mode, automatically pair jev's recorded recommendation against the gate's existing frontmatter verdict with no additional prompt to anyone. Once a gate goes live, ask short yes/no questions about the small number of cases that skipped human review, at most weekly, showing jev's own answer only after the human's answer.
for: During shadow mode this collects a label for every single gate signature that already happens today, at zero additional cost to the owner, because the frontmatter verdict already exists for an unrelated reason and is read a second time for this purpose (R3-process §3, describing zero added owner burden).

This option's live-period design follows the anchoring-avoidance ordering R4-calib's review recommends — showing the case first and jev's recommendation only after an independent answer is given (R4-calib §2). No separate wording or interface decision is needed beyond following that same ordering rule consistently. R4-calib's review recommends this exact ordering as the standard way to avoid the anchoring effect it separately identifies.

Limiting the live-period prompt to once per week and treating no-answer as a neutral, denominator-excluded state avoids silently counting silence as agreement, which R3-process's review flags as a risk of any unbounded feedback design (R3-process §3). A weekly cap also bounds the total number of times the owner can be asked something under this option's live-period mechanism. R3-process's review frames an unbounded feedback design, one with no cap on frequency, as carrying the same unanswered-prompt risk this option's cap is meant to avoid.

The shadow-mode half of this design requires no new prompt-writing or prompt-timing decisions at all, since it reuses a field format (the frontmatter verdict) that already exists and is already produced by every gated feature today. That existing field was already being produced for the gate's own purposes before any jev integration existed.
against: The auto-paired shadow-mode label depends on the frontmatter verdict being trustworthy as genuinely human-or-fallback-agent-authored; until the verdict-authorship guard examined in a separate fork exists, every such label is marked unverified and excluded from any graduation-threshold calculation, meaning this mechanism alone does not immediately produce usable samples.

Once a gate is live, human review of automatically-routed cases becomes voluntary by design, and R4-calib's review states voluntary review is not randomly distributed; the weekly-batch mechanism this option adds does not, by itself, guarantee the spot-check coverage rate needed to counteract that bias unless a separate minimum spot-check floor is also adopted (R4-calib §0.2, §5). R4-calib's review recommends a spot-check floor as a necessary addition precisely because this option's weekly-batch mechanism does not itself guarantee one.

This design produces two structurally different collection mechanisms — automatic pairing in shadow, active prompting in live — rather than one consistent mechanism throughout, which is more moving parts to specify, test, and keep synchronized than a single uniform approach. Specifying, testing, and keeping two mechanisms synchronized is more implementation surface than a single mechanism used consistently throughout.

The shadow-mode auto-pairing half of this design captures only what a human or fallback agent already happened to conclude for an unrelated purpose (approving the gate), not necessarily what they would conclude if asked specifically and directly about jev's recommendation. That gap between what was concluded and what would have been concluded if asked directly is not measurable under this option's own design.

C.description: Do not collect any human feedback labels at all, in shadow mode or after going live. Instead, use jev's own reported confidence values, aggregated across recorded calls, as the basis for deciding when a gate has accumulated enough evidence to graduate to automatic routing without a human label.
for: It has zero collection cost to the owner in every mode, shadow or live, since no prompt of any kind — automatic pairing, weekly batch, or per-feature question — is ever presented to anyone. No other option in this fork achieves zero cost in both shadow and live modes simultaneously.

It removes the anchoring-effect surface R4-calib's review identifies entirely, since there is no human answer for jev's own recommendation to anchor, because no human answer is ever collected under this option (R4-calib §2). That absence of an anchor is a structural property of collecting no label at all, not a design choice that could fail. R4-calib's review identifies this same anchoring risk as a live concern for the other two options in this fork, but not for this one.

It avoids the source-attribution bookkeeping the other two options require (distinguishing human, fresh-agent-reviewer, owner-self-review, and unverified labels), since no external label of any kind is being recorded under this option (R4-calib §1, describing that bookkeeping as unused here). Simpler bookkeeping is a genuine implementation advantage, independent of whether the underlying confidence-only approach is otherwise sound.

It has no dependency on the verdict-authorship guard examined elsewhere in this evaluation, since it never reads or relies on the frontmatter verdict field that guard is designed to make trustworthy. That independence also means this option's implementation timeline does not wait on that guard's own completion. That same independence also means a later decision to add a verdict-authorship guard would not require revisiting anything already built under this option.
against: TypeSafe's own documentation states calibration is measured only across groups of predictions and does not guarantee an individual answer is correct; graduating purely on jev's self-reported confidence, without ever checking that confidence against an independent human judgment, has no mechanism to detect whether jev is actually well-calibrated for these specific gates (research-jev.md §7, quoting the documentation verbatim). That gap applies specifically to this use case, since the documentation's own caveat is about calibration in aggregate, not about any one deployment.

TypeSafe publishes no official numeric threshold for the confidence field at all; the only concrete numeric thresholds found anywhere in TypeSafe's documentation apply to the `noul` and `score` fields in one cookbook, not to `confidence`, leaving no official basis for what confidence value should count as sufficient under this option (research-jev-api.md §8).

Every threshold design examined elsewhere in this evaluation is built around comparing jev's recommendation to an independent human-or-fallback-agent label; this option removes the only data source that comparison depends on, which none of the four reviews propose as sufficient on its own (R4-calib §1-§4). No comparison data of any kind would exist under this option, even if someone later wanted to check retroactively whether it had been sound.

Because no independent label is ever collected under this option, there is no data available afterward to check whether jev's confidence values were in fact well-calibrated for these particular gates, even retroactively, since the comparison data this fork's other options would have produced does not exist at all.
